The seeded variant sweep must check BOTH criteria destructible removal can regress -- distinct spawn cells and opening concealment (the map-variants plan's proof covers why room cannot regress). Dropping the concealment arm lets a seeded draw that removes the one block hiding two spawns from each other validate clean, so a catalog entry could advertise seeded-destructible variants whose actual draws reopen opening sightlines. Invisible on the shipped catalog either way: its full sweep (75 draws: 5 entries x N in {2,3,4} x 5 pinned seeds) already measures 0 failures, so only a fixture whose sight blocker is itself destructible can discriminate. A raw subtraction reads an angle a hair under +pi and one a hair over -pi as most of a full turn rather than 0.06 rad apart, so every tank tracking through due west would break its hold every tick and the layer would silently stop working in exactly one bearing. angleDelta is the same helper slewAngle uses, so the two cannot disagree about what 'close' means.

Without the decrement the span never expires: a hold armed once is held for the rest of the round, so the tank stops re-solving entirely rather than dwelling and re-aiming. That is a far larger behaviour change than the one measured, and it would read as an AI that has stopped tracking rather than one that has stopped twitching.

Pins the WIRING, not the helper: holdAimFor can be correct and fully unit-tested while decideAi quietly discards its result, which would leave every unit test in aim-hold.test.ts green and the shipped game completely unchanged. The write-back pair is deliberately left intact here so the mutation is a pure 'result ignored', not a type error. Failure count went 2 -> 3 when issue #371 added dispatch.test.ts's barrel-arrival case, which also depends on the held angle reaching the trigger.

The headline issue #245 defect: a developer session's WRITES land on the production keys, so a dev level jump, sandbox event or achievement check overwrites the real player's campaign. Only setItem is unnamespaced here -- reads still go through the prefix -- which is what makes it destructive rather than obviously broken: the developer session boots at defaults, writes over the player's save, and nothing in that session ever displays the collision. 10 of 40 tests in storage.test.ts, spanning the write/read-back pair, removeItem and clear scoping, enumeration, injectivity, the whole-inventory sweep, the reload round trip and the save.ts export/import case. The wide population is the point rather than noise: every property the adapter exists to provide is downstream of setItem landing in the right namespace.

The single most damaging thing this adapter could do wrong, and the reason clear() is scoped at all rather than delegated: an unscoped clear() on a developer session wipes the player's real save AND every neighbouring key on the origin this game shares with the rest of austinorphan.com (see save.ts). Killed by exactly one case, 'clears only its own namespace', 1 of 40 -- and only by its assertion on the surviving BASE keys: names() iterates the base, so an emptied base makes the adapter's own `length` read 0 either way and the length assertion alone would still pass.

key(i) must answer the STORE-FACING name inside the namespace, not the base storage's raw key at that index. Delegating to the base leaks both directions at once: a developer session enumerating storage sees the production keys it must not know about, and sees its own keys under their `tanks.dev.`-prefixed underlying names, so key(i) stops inverting setItem. Nothing in src/ walks a Storage by index today -- save.ts works from the SAVE_KEYS allow-list -- which is precisely why this needs a manifest entry rather than trust. 2 of 40 in storage.test.ts: the scoped-enumeration case and the injectivity case that round-trips every store key back out through key(i).

Drops the production short-circuit, so an ordinary URL gets a WRAPPER instead of the browser's own Storage object. Every key-addressed method still behaves identically (namespacedKey is the identity in production), so round-trip assertions stay green -- but `length`, `key(i)` and `clear()` would then filter on the developer prefix and report a production session as empty, and '#245: ordinary URLs retain current key names and behavior' stops being provable by identity and becomes an argument about wrapper equivalence. Killed only by the identity assertion 'hands back the SAME object', 1 of 40, which is the assertion that entry exists to keep load-bearing. `false as boolean` (the device storage-resolver-ignores-the-host already uses) keeps the mutation type-valid instead of a comparison tsc would reject; measured at `tsc --noEmit` exit 0 under the mutation, so the verdict is about test coverage rather than the compiler.

Applies the tidier `tanks.dev.progress.v1` mapping that the doc comment above DEVELOPER_KEY_PREFIX rejects, instead of prefixing the whole key. It is self-consistent -- read, write, remove and clear all agree on it -- so no single store's round trip breaks, and that self-consistency is exactly why it needs pinning: what it costs is the INVERSE, because names() strips only the prefix and hands back `progress.v1` where the store wrote `tanks.progress.v1`, and two store keys differing only by a leading `tanks.` would collapse onto one underlying key. 3 of 40 in storage.test.ts: the write-lands-under-the-prefix case, the scoped-enumeration case, and the injectivity/inverse case.

Pins the SELECTOR, not the adapter: a correct, fully covered createNamespacedStorage is worth nothing if no session ever asks for the developer namespace. Under this mutation `?dev=1` persists into the real player's keys exactly as it did before issue #245, and every adapter case above still passes because the adapter itself is untouched -- measured, 3 of 40, and the three are the developer rows of selectStorageNamespace's table (`?dev=1`, `?dev`, `?dev=1&aimRay=1`). The ternary keeps parseDeveloperMode's result and `search` read so the mutation compiles under the repo's noUnusedLocals/noUnusedParameters (the same device as preview-drops-the-rotate-buttons); measured at `tsc --noEmit` exit 0 under the mutation. Directional, and deliberately so: this mutation under-triggers, so the production rows and the 'is the `dev` GATE, not any individual flag' case cannot see it, and no entry in this manifest currently mutates the selector in the over-triggering direction.

The OVER-triggering half of the selector, which `storage-namespace-never-selects-developer` deliberately cannot see. This is the more damaging direction of the two: an ordinary URL would start persisting into `tanks.dev.*`, so the player's campaign, stats and achievements would still be on disk but invisible to the game -- indistinguishable from a wiped save, and silent. Killed by the production rows of selectStorageNamespace's table and by the `dev` GATE case, none of which the under-triggering entry reaches.

Isolation has a read half as well as a write half, and `storage-developer-writes-land-on-production-keys` only pins the write. Under this mutation a developer session WRITES to `tanks.dev.*` but READS the player's real keys, so it adopts the production campaign, the production legacy touch settings, and exports production data through save.ts -- while every write-side assertion still passes. `String(key)` rather than `key` so the mutation keeps the argument coercion the adapter does and differs only in the namespace mapping.

The one unpinned line issue #245 adds. `createNamespacedStorage` and `selectStorageNamespace` can both be correct and fully covered while this line never asks for the developer namespace, in which case `?dev=1` persists into the real player's keys exactly as before. Splits the session across two namespaces: the six stores land on the base keys while `AppSettings.storage` -- what save.ts and the `__tanks` dev console get -- stays namespaced. Every storage.ts adapter test still passes, because the adapter is untouched; only the wiring is wrong. The obvious "make PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE an override" edit, which prerequisites.test.ts already names in prose as this case's negative control. PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE is a PREFERENCE, not an override: a stale or mistyped value must not stop capture from finding a working install, and the aggregate failure must list every specifier it tried. Under the mutation a contributor whose PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE points at a moved install is told "Playwright with Chromium is required" with only that one dead path under `Tried:`, while a perfectly good ambient `playwright` is never attempted. Killed by `treats PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE as the first candidate and still tries the bare specifier` (#353), the only case that reads the second `Tried:` line -- 1 of the file's 4 cases; the other 3 pass under it, which is what expectFailures pins. First two manifest entries outside `src/`: the harness's own `vitest related` preflight relates tools/capture/prerequisites.test.ts to this file, so a tools/ target is measured exactly like a src/ one. Measured in both worlds this repo actually runs in, because Playwright is deliberately not a declared dependency: with node_modules/playwright{,-core} present (the documented local capture setup) and with them absent (CI's `verify` job, which installs Playwright only in the separate `visual` job). The second `Tried:` line's TEXT differs between them (`Chromium executable is missing at /missing/chromium` where playwright resolves, `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` where it does not); the line is PRESENT either way, which is why the assertion -- and this entry -- read the same in both.

The change issue #353's third acceptance criterion asks to be named: `loadPlaywright` stops naming the pinned version in its remediation. The message then tells a contributor to run `npm i --no-save playwright` unpinned, npm resolves whatever is latest, and the next capture run trips loadPlaywright's OWN version check a few lines up (`Playwright <x> is installed, but CI and capture require <CI_PLAYWRIGHT_VERSION>`) -- guidance that sends the reader in a circle instead of to the install CI uses. Killed by the rejection assertion in `ties capture documentation and errors to the canonical CI Playwright pin`, 1 of the file's 4 cases: that case's earlier assertions read ci.yml and README.md and still pass, and the other 3 cases never inspect the remediation text. The `\n` in `find`/`replace` is two literal bytes inside a template literal, not a newline. First two manifest entries outside `src/`: the harness's own `vitest related` preflight relates tools/capture/prerequisites.test.ts to this file, so a tools/ target is measured exactly like a src/ one. Measured in both worlds this repo actually runs in, because Playwright is deliberately not a declared dependency: with node_modules/playwright{,-core} present (the documented local capture setup) and with them absent (CI's `verify` job, which installs Playwright only in the separate `visual` job). `playwright@<version>` appears nowhere else in the aggregate message in either world, so deleting it here is what makes the case fail rather than an environment fact -- which is the whole point of #353, where the same case passed or failed on whether Playwright happened to resolve.

The whole reason `.ui-btn` has size MODIFIERS rather than a size: the pause panel's Mute and the three toggles beside it are a smaller control than the slab a panel stacks, and flattening the two into one size is the tidy-looking edit that erases the distinction. Every button still looks themed under this mutation -- `.ui-btn` supplies fill, text colour and cursor either way -- so `never lets a button fall through to browser default styling` stays green and only `keeps each size of quiet control to ONE size` notices, because that case measures each size group against the OTHER group as well as against itself. Without its final `not.toBe`, the two loops would both pass on a stylesheet that gave every button in the HUD one shape.

A button built without the primitive -- the shape of the defect #321 exists to remove, where `.hud-achievements-open` shipped with no base rule and rendered as a stock grey browser button beside three themed siblings. Two cases catch it and they catch DIFFERENT things: `never lets a button fall through to browser default styling` sees the rendering (the level buttons keep their own size rule, so they lose only fill, text colour and cursor), and `groups every button under a primitive` sees the omission itself, which is the property that still holds for a control whose own rule happens to cover everything. The second is what replaces `a new button joins by adding its selector to the group` now that the group is gone.

Exactly the state the HUD was in before #321: the selection ring is drawn and nothing is announced, so which choice is current is carried by a white border and by nothing else. `setSelected` exists to make the two channels inseparable, and this mutation separates them again by writing the state to a `data-` attribute instead: the value is still recorded, still moves with the choice, and is still invisible to every assistive technology. The class toggle is untouched, so every visual assertion in the suite stays green. Killed by three unit cases in ui.test.ts and by the two HUD sweeps over all 50 choice controls. COUNT MOVED 5 -> 7 for issue #281: the per-slot TEAM buttons are choice controls built with `setSelected`, so the two cases that read their `aria-pressed` -- the untouched slot showing its EFFECTIVE team, and a chosen team surviving a round trip through FFA -- detect this defect as well. Re-measured on the tree, not predicted; the harness reported the mismatch and the declaration was corrected to what it actually trips.

`aria-describedby=""` looks like absence and is not: it is still a described-by relationship, one that resolves to no element, which assistive technology reports as a broken reference rather than as a control needing no explanation. The distinction is invisible to any assertion that asks whether the reason is GONE by reading the attribute's value, which is why the cases here ask `hasAttribute` instead. Killed in ui.test.ts and in the versus-preview sweep, where the standalone Controllers panel's interactive buttons must carry no reference at all. Issue #260 raised this from 3 to 5: the versus pane's Start button now carries its refusal through the same helper, so two more assertions -- the pane's own aria-describedby checks -- fail when it is broken.

find: const p = snap || revived ? undefined : prevT;
why: Restores the defect #239 fixed: with only the world-wide `snap` left, a VS stock respawn -- which keeps the tank's id and does NOT restart the round -- interpolates the revived tank from the position it died at to the spawn point selected for it, and drags the spawn ring parented to its group along with it. Nothing else in the file notices: the tank is at the right place again one tick later, so every assertion about what a respawn LOOKS like a frame after the edge stays green, which is why the alpha sweep reads the first frame at four alphas rather than at one.

The over-correction, and the reason the teleport is read per tank rather than raised into the world-level `snap` beside `roundStartTick`: snapping unconditionally freezes every tank in the arena onto its current-tick pose, so nothing in the game interpolates at all and motion becomes a 60 Hz stutter. It is invisible to any test that renders a single alpha or a single tank, which is what `snaps only the revived tank: the other player keeps interpolating on the same sync` exists for -- and `interpolates normally within a round` catches the same thing from the pre-#239 side of the file.

Widens the application backdrop by ONE surface, which is the mistake this gate is most likely to be made into: `.hud-splash`'s own rule already keys on `atLaunch`, so folding the ground into it looks like consistency. It is not -- the title screen is deliberately a 0.92 scrim over the live arena ('the game is visibly already there, waiting'), and an opaque ground under it removes the only place the game is shown before it starts. The same one-surface widening applied to `paused` or an outcome screen would hide the board the player is reading the panel over, which is why hud.test.ts sweeps all six surfaces rather than sampling. RE-CUT for issue #364: the gate moved from a bare `appGroundEl.classList.toggle('ui-app-ground--hidden', !atMainMenu)` into the one transition contract's desired-state list, so the old anchor stopped applying -- which only `failed-to-apply` reported, while a grep for the status word read the run as fine. Same mutation, inverted sense: the list says which surfaces should be OPEN, so widening is `|| atLaunch` rather than `&& !atLaunch`. Scoped to hud.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

Leaves the landing a quit owes outstanding forever. `switchTo` is the ONE site that can settle the debt, because it is the one site that builds a world; without the clear, a Levels pick after a quit builds the picked board and the debt survives it, so the next Continue silently builds the campaign board over the level the player chose -- one extra world and one extra gameplay seed, on a gesture whose whole guarantee is that it enters what is already there. The alternative shape, clearing the flag at each of the three call sites that could satisfy it, is what `switchTo`'s own comment says did not hold by hand.

Swaps build-then-reveal for reveal-then-build. Both statements still run, so a test that only counts worlds and seeds cannot see it -- what changes is that `enterGameplay` is handed the STALE `currentSession`, the one resolved against the world the player abandoned, and the state change that hides the application ground reaches the screen before the landing board exists. The visible half is a frame of the abandoned board; the recorded half is a resolved session that does not describe the world underneath it. Ordering is the property the comment at this site claims, so it gets an entry rather than a promise.

Turns the application ground into a scrim, which is the failure the rest of issue #317 depends on not happening: the quit no longer rebuilds the board, so whatever world the player abandoned is still behind this layer -- a paused explosion under the New Game button if it is translucent. CSS is typechecked by nothing and read by no other test, the same silent-loss class the topbar safe-area entry above exists for, and the value is a token, so the loss would be one character in one line. hud.css.test.ts asserts opacity FIRST and the tuned value second for exactly this ordering of what matters.

The shipped behaviour issue #367 reverses, restored exactly: countdown ticks bank toward the profile's reaction delay, so an enemy that watched the player through the announced fire-free phase fires on the first live tick. Measured over the golden trace's population under this mutation: in 12 of the 30 traced runs an enemy stood at or past its full authored span the moment the countdown ended. Not a subtle regression to leave to a reviewer's eye -- it is the difference between a telegraphed first shot and an instant one, and the player has no counterplay to the second.

EQUIVALENT on the shipped tree, and the entry exists to say which fact makes it so. `canAct` is `phase === 'live'` while GRACE_TICKS is 0 (constants.ts), so today the two expressions are identical and no test can tell them apart -- this entry is the measurement that says so out loud instead of leaving the reader to wonder whether the choice was arbitrary. It stops being equivalent the moment grace is re-enabled, which that constant's own comment describes as a one-number change: grace is a phase in which tanks move and hunt but may not fire, and the rule this implements is 'start at LIVE acquisition', not 'start when firing is allowed'. A test that killed this today would have to fabricate a positive GRACE_TICKS, which pins a phase the game does not currently ship.

The same defect at the mirror site. `applyPlayerInput` already refuses the shot during the countdown (world.ts), which is exactly why this clock needed gating separately: the refusal hides the banking, and the scripted player emerges from the countdown entitled to fire on the first live tick. Without an entry here the enemy half is pinned and the player half is not, which is the asymmetry issue #367's own acceptance criterion ('every shipped profile') rules out.

The SPAN is half the rule and the easiest half to drop, because dropping it leaves a tree that still holds a plan, still falls back, and still passes any test that only checks which angle came out. What it removes is the commitment: the plan would turn over on EVERY tick its preferred type has no solution, which is the churn issue #332 exists to stop -- teal would flip back and forth for as long as the player stayed behind cover. Deleting the `lapsed &&` term must fail a test, or the profile field is decorative.

find: nextAimHeld: null, nextAimHeldTicks: 0, nextShotPlan: holdPlan, nextShotPlanTicks };
why: This is the defect found while shipping the issue, kept as a guard. stepAi writes the pair back only when the decision CARRIES one, so a return path that omits it does not error -- it silently freezes the countdown for every tick the arena has no live player, i.e. every countdown and every player death, making the real span longer than shotCommitmentTime authorises. The prototype shipped this bug and every measurement taken on it described a span the profile did not control.

find: const nextShotPlanTicks = lapsed ? Math.round(cfg.ai.shotCommitmentTime * TICK_HZ) : planTicks - 1;
why: The shipped profile authorises 2.0s = 120 ticks, EXACTLY the value of the prototype constant the field replaced -- so a test that asserts 120 against the shipped roster cannot tell a live profile read from a pin, and every acceptance criterion about a validated per-profile field would be met on paper by a hardcoded number. Killing this requires a fixture that injects a DIFFERENT shotCommitmentTime, which is why one exists.

Pins the WIRING and the polarity of 'no opinion' in one mutation, the way the aim-hold entry pins its own. Inverted, teal's plan is never persisted (the countdown never advances, so the span never elapses) while brown's and grey's decisions -- which never evaluate a plan -- would clear a plan the tank still holds. teal.test.ts probes tealDecision directly and stays entirely green either way, so only a dispatcher-level test can catch this.

find: const preferBank = heldPlan === null ? true : heldPlan === 'bank';
replace: const preferBank = heldPlan === null ? false : heldPlan === 'bank';
why: The never-held default is invisible on most geometry: where only one shot type solves, both defaults fall through to the same angle and the same stored plan, so an assertion taken on open ground passes under either value. It is only observable where BOTH types solve -- which is the fixture this entry forces to exist, and the reason that fixture does not reuse the open-field helper the neighbouring tests use.

This exact mutation SURVIVED the whole suite before the seam was extracted -- measured, not supposed. Without the VS branch a versus session falls back to the derived positional rule, so bots land in the LAST slots regardless of where the player put them and the pane's displayed assignment is silently discarded at Start. That is the precise defect issue #260 opens with, and it is invisible to every test that only checks a match starts.

Pins 'developer flags and player setup cannot create competing assignment sources'. Left un-derived, a ?bots=3 in the URL and a pane showing one bot are two live answers to one question, and which one a consumer believes depends on whether it reads the count or the roles. Deriving the count from the roles makes them agree by construction rather than by convention.

The highest-risk surface in this change, and the failure is a LAUNCH one rather than a wrong pixel: resolveVersusConfig THROWS both for an id naming no catalog entry and for a real id whose entry does not support the (players, mode) being started. Both are reachable from stored data alone -- an arena retired between builds, or a two-player map stored before four players were chosen -- so an unvalidated read turns a stale save into a game that will not start.

'random' names no catalog entry, so a catalog-backed predicate refuses it. Without the explicit allowance every read converts the draw-for-me sentinel into a concrete board -- permanently, and silently. VersusConfig.arenaId's own doc comment is emphatic that the UNRESOLVED config is what the pane reopens with; this entry is that contract's guard at the persistence boundary.

find: for (let i = 0; i < players; i++) out.push(slots[i] ? { ...slots[i] } : defaults[i]);
replace: for (let i = 0; i < players; i++) out.push(defaults[i]);
why: Rebuilding rather than resizing throws away every role the player set as soon as they touch the player-count buttons, which is a silent loss of exactly the choices this issue exists to preserve. Worth pinning because the array still ends up the right LENGTH, so every shape-based assertion keeps passing. Issue #260 raised this from 3 to 4, and the extra failure is the point: until the pane had role CONTROLS, nothing in the UI could show a discarded role. The fourth test drives the player-count buttons and reads the role back off the rendered card, so this is now pinned end to end rather than at the model alone.

Insets the shell by its COLLISION radius instead of its DRAWN nose reach -- the intuitive fix for issue #237, and the one that does not work: it leaves the visible nose 0.225 past the barrel opening, so the daylight pop the issue is about survives untouched. Worth pinning because the shell still spawns behind the plane, so every symbolic SHELL_SPAWN_FORWARD assertion in the tree stays green; only the two assertions that constrain the inset's SIZE can see it.

find: return { spawn, flash: vadd(owner.pos, vscale(dir, SHELL_MUZZLE_FORWARD)) }
why: Drags the muzzle flash inward with the shell, so the gun visibly discharges from inside itself -- particles.ts bursts on the fire event's pos and is the only consumer that reads it. Pinned because the event still carries a plausible point on the firing line, which no shape or type check can distinguish from the right one.

Asks whether the BARREL OPENING is clear rather than whether the region the shell will occupy is -- the exact confusion splitting the two constants introduced. It both refuses shots that fit and, worse, misses a wall sitting in the span the shell is actually born into, which spawns a live shell inside solid geometry.

When the shell cannot be born at the barrel and retreats to the tank centre, this leaves the flash out on the opening -- bursting inside the wall that caused the retreat, off a gun that produced nothing there this tick. The retreat still happens and the shell still spawns safely, so only an assertion on the event's position sees it.

The failure mode SHELL_NOSE_REACH_RADII exists to catch: src/sim may not import src/render, so a renderer retune can silently desynchronise the spawn depth from the drawn geometry. Stands in for the next person shortening the shell without knowing the sim keyed an inset to its length.

Inverts resolveBulletHits' outbound exemption, so a tank is immune to its own returning ricochet and vulnerable to the shell it is currently firing. Load-bearing since issue #237: the spawn circle now overlaps the firer's own hull, and this guard is the only thing stopping a tank killing itself on the trigger pull.

stepMines decrements BEFORE it checks expiry, so the rendered countdown runs DELAY down to 1 and never 0. Dividing by DELAY tops the fill out at 29/30: the cue visibly never completes, and the acceptance criterion 'the final proximity-warning frame agrees with the blast-start tick' is violated by one tick in a way no screenshot review would reliably catch.

Both events would still make a sound, so 'the warnings are audible' stays true while the ONE thing issue #276 is about -- that a player can tell 'you tripped this' from 'time is running out' -- is destroyed. Pins the distinction rather than the presence.

find:
if (playerPos !== null && distance(e.pos, playerPos) <= MINE_DANGER_RADIUS) {
          vibrate(MINE_TRIP_PATTERN_MS);
why: Ungated, a mine tripped anywhere on the map buzzes this player's device -- the presence-only anti-pattern CLAUDE.md names, and the mechanism by which several simultaneous mines become the unbounded spam the issue asks us to prevent. The gate is also what makes the cue mean 'near YOU'.

Growth IS the fuse cue now that the blink is gone (owner ruling on PR #396): with the radius frozen the glow still appears, still brightens, and still ends exactly at the blast, so every timing assertion stays green while the thing that communicates urgency has stopped moving. Replaces the retired mine-fuse-ring-thickness-frozen, which anchored on a ring that no longer exists.

THE DIRECTION IS THE RULING. Inverting this reproduces the previous revision exactly -- a lit region growing from the centre outward instead of closing in from the rim -- using the same numbers read the other way round. Every timing assertion (starts empty, full on the blast frame, monotone) passes under both, so only an assertion about which EDGE moves can tell them apart.

replace: { const g = clamp01(1 - mine.timer / FUSE_WARNING_SECONDS); fuse = { growth: Math.floor(g * 12) % 2 === 0 ? g : g * 0.4 }; }
why: The blink was removed for a reason that outlives the aesthetic preference: sustained flashing above ~3 Hz is a photosensitivity hazard, and the previous revision could only BOUND it at 6 Hz rather than remove it. This entry reintroduces an oscillation and must fail, so the monotone guarantee is enforced rather than merely intended.

Decides compatibility from the field table instead of the content hash, so a recipe differing only outside that table -- its title, budget, timeout, or any field added since the table was written -- is accepted as the same measuring instrument. The hash is what identifies the reviewed configuration; this is the plausible-looking implementation that silently compares against an unreviewed recipe.

Drops the frame-count check, so two clips of different lengths are compared positionally and the surplus frames on the longer side are simply ignored. The issue rules this out by name: a comparison must not silently freeze, pad, truncate, or retime one side to conceal a mismatch, because the result looks exactly like a successful one.

Reports every run as having cleaned up. A leaked worktree needs a human and makes the command exit non-zero, so swallowing that is the failure mode this tool can least afford -- and it is the exact bug the original code had by returning from inside the try block, where the value was fixed before the finally block ran.

Removes the backstop behind 'never delete or reuse an existing user worktree': any path in the owned set is force-removed, wherever it points. With fifteen live worktrees on a development box, a poisoned or stale entry then destroys another session's work rather than being reported.

Puts the ref before the SHA again, so a long branch name pushes the commit identity off the right edge of the panel while the caption still looks plausible. Found by looking at a rendered frame rather than by reasoning about the code, which is why it is pinned rather than trusted to review.

find: await ffmpeg(['-i', basePng, '-i', headPng, '-filter_complex', '[0:v][1:v]blend=all_mode=difference', difference], deps);
replace: await ffmpeg(['-i', labelledBase, '-i', labelledHead, '-filter_complex', '[0:v][1:v]blend=all_mode=difference', difference], deps);
why: Differences the captioned frames instead of the originals. The two captions always differ -- they name different refs -- so the brightest region of every difference image becomes the label text, burying whatever actually changed in the render.

Stops asking capture to keep its raw PNGs, which is what the entire comparison is computed from -- analyseFrames reads <dir>/frames/ and would find nothing. Pinned because it genuinely survived: capture-runner is the seam every orchestrator test replaces with a fake, so dropping this flag left all 100 other tests green until the module got a test of its own.

`inspectPrerequisites` is the function capture and compare actually call, and until the broken-toolchain cases it had no test of its own: `prerequisites.test.ts` exercised `toolVersion` and `loadPlaywright` directly, while `orchestrate.test.ts` and `runner.test.ts` both replace `inspectPrerequisites` with a fake. The composition -- which tools get probed at all -- was the seam every caller stubs, so nothing covered it. Dropping the ffprobe probe and reporting FFmpeg's version in its place is what that hole looks like from the outside: the command claims to have verified an encoder it never ran. MEASURED: 2 of the 8 tests in prerequisites.test.ts fail -- 'names ffprobe specifically when that one is genuinely absent from PATH' (the mutant probes only ffmpeg, which the fixture PATH does supply, so nothing is rejected) and 'accepts the same toolchain once both encoders are on PATH, and reports what it found' (ffprobe comes back reading 'ffmpeg version 0.0-fixture'). Against the pre-existing tests for this file the same mutation SURVIVES.

Compare must check prerequisites in the environment it was HANDED, not the ambient one. In production those are the same object, which is exactly why dropping `deps.env ??` reads as a harmless simplification -- and why every test that injects a fake `inspectPrerequisites` is blind to it, since a fake ignores the argument. A session teardown that never stops its driver. The retired session's frame loop stays registered AND keeps stepping its own disposed world every frame, alongside the live session's -- two simulations advancing on one page after a single Campaign<->Versus switch. NOT new coverage: measured on origin/main, this mutation already failed 1 of 388, at 'stops the frame loop, so a queued callback cannot advance the world'. What issue #317 adds is the repeated-route view of the same defect -- 3 of 397 now, the pre-existing case plus 'leaves exactly one outstanding frame registration' and 'leaves exactly one frame loop still ADVANCING the world'. Failing BOTH of those is what separates this from `retired-session-frame-loop-never-cancelled`, which fails only the first; that contrast is measured, not assumed.

`stop()` clears its running flag but never cancels the frame it has already queued -- the guard is inverted so it can never fire. Strictly milder than `retired-session-keeps-advancing-the-world`: `frame`'s own `if (!running) return;` still makes the leaked callback inert, so the world does NOT advance twice and only the registration leaks. 1 of 397, at 'leaves exactly one outstanding frame registration' -- and NOT at 'leaves exactly one frame loop still ADVANCING the world', which is the whole reason both entries exist. This one is genuinely new coverage: run against origin/main's loop.test.ts the same mutation passes all 388 tests, because that rAF fake held a single `pending` callback slot and a no-op `cancel`, so one live frame loop and two were indistinguishable.

One cell of vs-tri-01's notch cheek turned from destructible to solid, breaking the mirror about column 13 that its notes claim (issue #272). RE-ANCHORED for issue #424's rework -- the previous find string named a row of a grid that no longer exists, which the harness reports as failed-to-apply, but only if someone runs it. Same shape as `duel-board-loses-its-rotational-symmetry` and for the same reason: the board still loads, still validates, and one flipped cell on a 27x17 board is invisible in a screenshot. What breaks is the FAIRNESS claim, which for the two base players is carried entirely BY the mirror: one of them now has a wall where the other has a breachable. Scoped to versus-catalog-rules.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

Bars vs-tri-01's row 11 across columns 9-17, closing the middle of the lower lateral lane. The point is NOT that a narrow gap appears -- narrow gaps are ordinary arena furniture and this board has them deliberately. The point is that closing a ROUTE is invisible to the cell metric and visible only to the tank one. MEASURED on this board: with the bar in place the authored cell distances stay at 26/26/26 and every cell-based claim -- mirror symmetry, the maximin spawn triangle, connectivity, spawn clearance, room, concealment and all ten seeded variants -- stays clean, while the distance a tank must actually drive changes. Exactly one assertion in the scoped file fails, and it is the tank-footprint lattice one. That gap between the two metrics is the defect issue #423 was opened for, and this entry is the proof the newer assertion is what closes it. RENAMED from `tri-board-passage-narrowed-to-one-cell`: the old name described the gap width, which is not the property being pinned. Scoped to versus-catalog-rules.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The topbar LIVES readout is the only projection of `world.lives`, and the constant it is replaced with is LIVES itself (balance.json `lives: 3`) -- so this mutation is invisible to any fixture whose board carries full lives. That was EVERY synthetic build until issue #386: `loop.test.ts`'s fake `levels.world` recorded its `lives` argument into `rec.levelBuilds` and then dropped it, spreading `opts.world ?? createArenaWorld(seed)` without stamping it, while the real `createWorldFor` does stamp it. Measured on a88d39e, before the fake was fixed: this exact mutation left 4008 of 4008 tests green across 170 of 170 test files -- the readout was unpinned repository-wide. The fake now applies `lives: lives ?? base.lives`, and THE STATED RESIDUAL test reads the readout across two builds whose arguments differ (a practice board taking arena.ts's own default, then Continue's run board carrying 2), so a constant can no longer satisfy both. Scoped to loop.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only. COUNT RE-MEASURED for issue #428: 1 -> 2, because the start-boundary suite reads the lives a fresh run was given, which is a second path through the same readout. The failing SET was compared, not the number renumbered.

The identity tint stops being applied per EMISSION, so a decal keeps whatever colour it was built with. Decals are pooled (`pool.pop() ?? makeDecal()`), so the visible defect is not 'no colour' -- it is a player inheriting ANOTHER player's tint the moment the pool turns over, which on a busy board is most marks. It looks like a working feature in a screenshot of a fresh round and wrong in play, and no assertion on `treadColorFor` alone can see it, since that function stays correct. Caught by the real-emit-path case and by the pool-turnover case that expires one player's marks before the other prints into them. Scoped to tread-trails.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only. The replacement is `void colorHex;` rather than an empty string: the manifest validator requires a non-empty `replace` (lib.mjs, "'replace' must be a non-empty string"), and a no-op that still consumes the parameter expresses the deletion without leaving an unused-argument diagnostic behind it.

The trail tint stops excluding `campaign-coop`, so a FOUR-PLAYER CO-OP campaign board prints identity-tinted trails. This is the exact defect the first implementation shipped and a screenshot caught: co-op clears the player-count gate -- four player tanks, four identity rings -- so `identityApplies` alone is not enough, and issue #284's scope says campaign trails stay neutral in the initial implementation. Single-player campaign is NOT the discriminating case here (it fails the player-count gate either way), which is why the test uses four co-op tanks and asserts the same four ARE tinted in ffa -- otherwise the case would pass against a build that tinted nothing. Scoped to tread-trails.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

One cell of vs-quad-01's right-hand rim block turned from solid to open floor, on the board's own row axis, breaking the column mirror its notes claim (issue #273). Same shape as `tri-board-loses-its-mirror-symmetry` and `duel-board-loses-its-rotational-symmetry`, and the same reason: the board still loads, still validates, still has four distinct and mutually concealed spawns at N=4, still passes clearance, connectivity and every seeded variant -- `versusCatalogEntryFailures` returns clean on it -- and one flipped cell on a 27x17 board is invisible in a screenshot. What breaks is the FAIRNESS claim, which for four players is carried ENTIRELY by the two mirrors: without them the four corners stop being one orbit of the symmetry group, and 'every spawn holds the same multiset of distances' becomes a coincidence rather than a construction. Scoped to versus-catalog-rules.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

Restores the exact defect issue #416 fixed: a code span that can only be seen when both backticks sit on one line. An opening backtick on one line and its closer on the next would again leave a `Parent: #N` mirror between them looking like prose, so an issue DOCUMENTING the form is audited as USING it -- a red required check whose remediation cannot be followed, because there is no parent to add. Nothing else observes it: the audit's other outputs are unchanged and the whole 181-issue corpus parses identically either way.

find: i += open; // unmatched: literal text, left exactly as written
replace:
for (let k = i; k < chars.length; k += 1) if (chars[k] !== '\n') chars[k] = ' ';
      break;
why: The over-correction #416 invited and this change deliberately refused: treating an unmatched backtick as an open span and blanking the rest of the body. CommonMark says a backtick run with no equal-length closer is literal text, so this would make the parser disagree with how GitHub renders the body it is reading, and would silently DROP real parent mirrors that merely happen to sit after a stray backtick. Pins the decision, not just the code.

Deletes findDependencyCycles' de-duplication outright. Before issue #417 added its test this SURVIVED -- all 25 tests in metadata.test.ts stayed green -- so the whole block was unverified production logic. It is genuinely reachable, but only narrowly: a duplicated BACK-edge, where the same blocker is listed twice pointing at a node still on the stack, because `visiting.get()` is consulted before `visited.has()`. A duplicated forward edge does not reach it, and neither does any of the 4096 directed graphs on 4 distinct nodes. Without the guard the audit reports one cycle as two errors, telling a maintainer to break an edge that has already been reported.

The whole point of issue #260's store is that the pane's choices survive a reload. Without this write the pane still LOOKS correct for the rest of the page-session -- every selection renders, Start carries it, the gate runs -- and forgets everything on the next load. That is invisible to any assertion made against a single HUD instance, which is why the persistence tests read back through a SECOND createHud over the same Storage.

The issue's 'never accept Start with an inert required slot'. The reasons would still render on the offending card, so the pane would still LOOK like it was refusing -- while Start stayed clickable and launched a match with an unassigned or driverless tank. Computing a refusal and not enforcing it is the failure this pins.

Derives every slot's device as if no controller were connected. A second human slot would read 'Unassigned' and refuse Start with a controller plugged in, and -- worse in kind -- the gate would stop reacting to a hotplug at all, which is the criterion about a disconnect disabling Start with an actionable reason.

find: problem !== null && problem.kind !== 'no-human' && problem.kind !== 'one-team' && problem.slot === slot;
why: Drops the slot check, so the FIRST problem's sentence is stamped on every card at once -- 'Player 2 is off' would appear under Player 3 as well. The pane deliberately shows one actionable reason at a time (versusSetupProblem returns the first problem, not a list); this pins that the other cards stay silent, which a test asserting only the offending card would not. RE-ANCHORED for issue #281: the guard gained a `problem.kind !== 'one-team'` clause when the team-count refusal joined `no-human` as the second PANE-level problem, so the previous find string no longer occurs -- which the harness reports as `failed-to-apply`, and which CI caught here rather than the local sweep, because the local selection was filtered to the files the change was ABOUT (`arena.ts`, `versus-setup.ts`) and this entry lives in `hud.ts`. The mutation, its meaning and its killing test are unchanged; only the anchor moved, and the count below was re-measured on the new text rather than carried over.

Issue #321's rule is that a disabled control's reason is ASSOCIATED, not merely nearby. The sentence would still be on screen for a sighted player while a screen-reader user hears only that Start is disabled. Nothing about the visible rendering changes, so only an aria-describedby assertion can catch it.

Leaves a refused control drawn exactly like a live one: `disabled` is still set and the gate still refuses, so every DOM assertion in the suite keeps passing and only the pixels lie. This is the defect that shipped in the first draft of issue #260 and was caught by photographing the built app -- Start was disabled and still bright green with its raised shadow. CSS is typechecked by nothing, so without this entry the whole treatment could be deleted silently.

Restores a real latent crash that typing this module under checkJs surfaced (issue #417). GitHub OMITS the parent key rather than sending null when an issue has none, so `parentLoaded: true` with no `parent` sent `auditOpenIssues` into `nativeParent.number` and threw TypeError. The audit runs on every issues event, so one such payload took down the required check for every issue in the run -- a stack trace instead of a remediation. Measured on the pre-fix tree: it threw; after, it reports declared-parent-missing-native.

The hover treatment applied on devices with no hovering pointer (issue #392). This is a correctness defect rather than a cosmetic one, and it is invisible on the machine that writes it: a touch device reports a tap as a hover and HOLDS it until the next tap lands elsewhere, so every control the player has touched stays looking pointed-at. Nothing in a desktop browser, a screenshot, or a jsdom computed-style read can see it -- jsdom does not recompute dynamic pseudo-classes at all, which is why the guard is checked as stylesheet TEXT. `@media all` is chosen over deleting the wrapper so the rules stay syntactically nested and only the CONDITION is wrong, which is the realistic form of this mistake. Scoped to hud.css.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

One hover selector loses `:not(:disabled)` (issue #392's second acceptance criterion). A locked level button -- `hud.ts` sets the real `disabled` attribute, and `.hud-level-btn--locked` dims it to 0.35 opacity -- would brighten under the pointer, telling the player a control they cannot activate is available. Worse than no hover at all, and the sort of thing that survives review because the rule LOOKS right; the selector is checked per-rule rather than by eye. Only the base `.ui-btn` selector is mutated: one is enough to prove the assertion sweeps every rule in the block rather than a named list. Scoped to hud.css.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

find: out.append(name, params.get(name) as string); // first-wins, as the parser reads it
why: The canonical URL resolves a duplicated developer parameter to the LAST value while every reader in devflags.ts resolves it to the first (`isOn`, `asSeed` and the rest all go through `URLSearchParams.get`, which returns the first). The result is the one thing this function must never produce: a canonical URL that PARSES DIFFERENTLY from the one the player supplied -- `?dev=1&quality=low&quality=high` would canonicalise to `quality=high` and silently change the render preset. Nothing about the output LOOKS wrong; both values came from the URL. It is caught by the first-wins case and by the round-trip sweep, which compares `parseDevFlags(canonical)` against `parseDevFlags(original)` rather than comparing the model to itself. Scoped to dev-config.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The playtest bundle reports itself as having FORCED a flag the URL asked for directly. A UI reading these notes would tell the player 'turned on by playtest, not requested directly' about a control they set themselves, and offer to remove a parameter that is doing real work. The mutation is invisible to any assertion that only checks the bundle's members are on -- they are, either way -- which is why the test compares the forced SET against `expandsTo` minus the directly-requested flag rather than counting. Scoped to dev-config.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

Drops the tank-egress rule out of the verdict while still computing and reporting it -- exactly the shape the defect took before issue #423. Keystone and Quarters passed clearance, connectivity, symmetry, path distance and scripted playtests and shipped unplayable: players could not leave their spawns. Every cell-based criterion stays green under this mutation, which is the point; only an assertion that a board with no tank-sized exit is UNSUITABLE catches it.

find: if (circleVsAABB({ x: (i + 0.5) * step, y: (j + 0.5) * step }, TANK_RADIUS, b).hit) legal[k] = 0;
replace: if (circleVsAABB({ x: (i + 0.5) * step, y: (j + 0.5) * step }, 0, b).hit) legal[k] = 0;
why: Shrinks the tank to a POINT, which is precisely what every pre-existing check did by reasoning about cell centres. A one-cell gap is 0.667 wide against a 1.0-wide tank and admits no legal centre position, but admits a point trivially -- so under this mutation the minimum-width fixture's 1-cell passage reads as passable and the boards that shipped unplayable read as fine. Pins that the footprint, not the topology, is what the rule measures. RE-ANCHORED after the wall-rasterisation rewrite: the original find string named the per-point wall loop that rewrite replaced, and it went stale without failing anything locally -- CI's failed-to-apply is what said so.

Stops refusing a spawn sealed by destructibles in a pocket too small to survive blowing it. Only a mine clears a destructible (destructibleByBlast, mines.ts) and a mine kills within MINE_BLAST_RADIUS + TANK_RADIUS = 2.5, so the player pays a LIFE to leave the start line -- which is exactly how Keystone shipped, whose spawn pockets measure 1.18 to 1.72 across. The solid-connectivity half of the gate does NOT catch it: Keystone's spawns are reachable once the destructibles are gone, so without this line the board reads as suitable again.

Puts the customize rotate buttons back to the 34px literal they carried before issue #352, which is below the 44 CSS px touch floor Apple/WCAG state and the repo declares as `--hud-control-min`. Nothing else notices: the board still renders, the cluster still fits on one row (it is 40px narrower, not wider), no layout moves that a screenshot diff would catch, and jsdom does no layout so no computed-size assertion anywhere in the suite can see it -- which is exactly why the guard this kills asserts the DECLARATION rather than the rendered box. Measured: KILLED, 1 of 50 in hud.css.test.ts, the 'sized to be hit' case. The token half of that guard is deliberately NOT the target here: lowering `--hud-control-min` itself would also resize `.hud-level-btn` and `.hud-swatch`, so it would be a different and broader defect; this entry isolates the one control the issue was about. Scoped to hud.css.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The optional call made mandatory -- the paint shop demanding a gameplay renderer again, which is the exact coupling issue #427 removed. This is the one line that decides whether Customize is an APPLICATION route or a gameplay one: `restyle` runs on every hull, skin and accent pick, and with no session there is no sink, so a non-optional call throws on a page whose only crime is having no match running. WHY IT NEEDS ITS OWN ENTRY, measured rather than assumed: with this mutation applied, `loop.test.ts` still passes 397 of 397. It cannot see the defect, because every route it reaches goes through `startGameWith`, which always attaches a sink -- so the whole existing suite agrees a session is present and the missing case is the one nobody was testing. `route-ui.test.ts` fails 2 of its 14: `the paint shop records a pick and drives the preview with NO renderer attached`, and `a detached sink stops the pushes without stopping the pick`, which is that case's own negative control (it re-runs the same pick after clearing the sink, so a build that pushed a triple regardless of the sink would fail there too). Two failures, MEASURED by applying this edit and running the file, not predicted. Scoped to route-ui.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only. COUNT MOVED 2 -> 3 for issue #427: the combined case that drives every route handler against a real empty `GameSessionHost` fires `onPickSkin`, so a mandatory style sink throws there as well as in the two paint-shop cases. Re-measured on the tree, not predicted.

The chosen control drawn with the SAME border style as an unchosen one, under forced colours. This is the defect issue #368 was opened over, restored: measured in Chromium before the contract existed, `.ui-selectable`'s base `2px solid transparent` comes back OPAQUE and identical to `--on`'s authored white on both the dark and light high-contrast themes, so the ring the primitive's own comment calls "the ONLY visual signal of the current choice" disappears and every swatch, skin, source and option reads as selected. `border-color: Highlight` is deliberately LEFT in place by this mutation rather than removed with it, because colour alone is not the contract: `.hud-swatch` carries `forced-color-adjust: none` (the colour on a swatch is its content), so on a swatch the ring's colour is unforced and can land on a same-coloured Canvas -- the shape is the channel that holds in both cases. Nothing outside forced-colors mode moves, so no ordinary-rendering guard can see it, and jsdom never matches the media query at all, so no computed-style assertion can either. Killed by the text-level pair in `hud.css.test.ts` that asserts unselected is dotted, selected is solid, and the two differ. Scoped to hud.css.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The one narrow opt-out moved onto a CONTAINER, which is the failure mode `forced-color-adjust` invites: the property inherits, so `none` on `.hud-panel` takes every descendant out of colour forcing with it -- the whole interface silently stops honouring the user's high-contrast palette while still passing a rule sweep that only asks whether the declaration exists. Issue #368's boundaries name this explicitly ("No wholesale forced-color-adjust: none") and its criterion 5 requires any use to be narrowly scoped and justified. The swatch is the justified case and the only one: `hud.ts` sets each swatch's fill inline from the palette, so forcing replaces all eleven with a single system colour and the hull and accent pickers stop offering a choice rather than merely looking different. Killed by the guard that asserts `forced-color-adjust` appears exactly once in the whole file AND that its owning selector is `.hud-swatch` -- the count alone would pass this mutation, since it moves the declaration rather than adding one. Scoped to hud.css.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The exact state this rule was added to fix, restored. `.hud-swatch` carries `forced-color-adjust: none` because on a colour swatch the colour IS the content -- but opting out means the agent stops replacing THIS element's colours, so `.ui-selectable`'s base ring keeps its authored `transparent` and an unchosen near-white swatch has no boundary at all against a light high-contrast theme's white Canvas. WHY THIS ENTRY EARNS ITS PLACE ALONGSIDE THE OTHER TWO: those pin collapses that `tools/uikit/forced-colors.mjs` measured and reported. This one pins the class that probe COULD NOT catch -- every computed reading was correct while the bug was live, because a transparent border is precisely what the unforced stylesheet asks for and the opt-out is what makes it survive into forced-colors mode. It was found by looking at the capture after the numbers all read clean, which is the only way it could have been. The repair works because a system keyword still resolves inside an opted-out subtree: the opt-out stops the agent REPLACING colours, it does not stop `CanvasText` meaning what it means. Killed by the guard that requires the unchosen swatch to name `border-color` AND to name a system keyword rather than an authored colour -- asserting the property alone would pass this mutation, since it keeps the declaration and only changes its value. Scoped to hud.css.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

A track position written out longhand at the consumer instead of taken from the shared model -- the exact shape `makeTank` had before issue #385, and the way an exported tank silently stops being the tank the game draws. The tracks move from the model's +/-0.375 (HULL_WIDTH/2 - TRACK_W/2) to +/-0.3, which pulls them visibly inward off the hull's edge. WHY THIS ENTRY EXISTS RATHER THAN A COMPARISON OF THE TWO BUILDERS: `makeTank` calls `tankParts()`, so a test that checked the model against itself would be comparing a function to its own output and could not fail. The risk is at the CONSUMER, and it is measured: with this mutation applied, `src/render/entities.test.ts` passes 90 of 90 -- the whole existing render suite is blind to it, because nothing there asserts where a track sits -- while `tank-model.test.ts` fails 1 of 7, on the case that compares the live scene graph's track offsets against the model's. That gap between 90-of-90 green and one named failure is the coverage this issue added. Scoped to tank-model.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

`normal` stops returning its INPUT and starts returning an equal copy. Both issues #267 and #223 require normal to be the exact no-op -- #223's criterion says 'Normal produces byte-identical/no-op profile resolution' -- and this mutation is the shape that quietly breaks it: every value is still identical, so any `toEqual` assertion passes, and a reader of the diff sees a harmless-looking spread. What it costs is the guarantee that a `normal` bot cannot differ from a pre-#267 bot even by object shape, which is what makes the whole feature additive over a config saved before difficulty existed. Killed by the identity case, which asserts `toBe` across every shipped tank kind AND for an omitted argument -- the form every existing `decidePlayerInput` caller uses. Scoped to bot-difficulty.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The accuracy ceiling raised until it cannot bind, which is how `hard` becomes the oracle both issues forbid by name ('No preset may create oracle-perfect awareness or aim'). It is a SILENT defect on the shipped data: the player profile is STATIC_BASIC at aimAccuracy 0.55, so `hard` lands at 0.6875 and the clamp never fires -- every difficulty still behaves plausibly and no shipped configuration looks wrong. The clamp only matters for a profile near the bound, which is why the test exercises a synthetic one at 0.99 rather than only the shipped one; testing the shipped profile alone would leave the clamp itself unexercised and this mutation alive. Both spreads are an anchor DIVIDED by accuracy, so an unbounded accuracy drives the seeded error to nothing. Scoped to bot-difficulty.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

Every bot plays at Normal whatever the player picked -- the selector still renders, still shows a selection, still writes the descriptor, and the setup still persists; only the match ignores it. WHY THIS ENTRY EXISTS AT THIS SITE: an earlier shape passed the preset as `decidePlayerInput`'s fifth argument at the frame-loop call, and replacing THAT with the default was measured to leave 1801 tests green -- nothing in the tree drives a bot far enough for its aim spread to be observable, so the whole feature could have shipped dead with a full suite behind it. The preset is now closed over inside `createBotSources`, which removes the argument a caller could drop and leaves exactly one place it can still be lost: this line. Killed by the two cases that read the returned source's `difficulty` per slot, including the un-configured slot that must resolve Normal through ABSENCE rather than through this fallback being the only path. Scoped to loop.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The versus roster falls back to the `slot % 2` derivation and ignores what the player chose -- which is issue #281's whole defect restored, and it goes SILENTLY: the board still loads, every tank still carries a team, and a 2v2 still looks like a 2v2. What breaks is that it is not the 2v2 the setup pane displayed. The mutation is invisible to any assertion that only checks `team` is defined, or that two teams exist, because the derivation produces exactly that. Killed by the pair in `arena.test.ts` that configures `[0, 0, 1, 2]` -- a THREE-team split the alternating derivation cannot produce at all, so agreement cannot be coincidental -- and by the sparse case, which pins that an unset slot still derives. Deliberately does NOT touch the campaign co-op stamp or the FFA path: FFA never stamps `Tank.team` (types.ts), which is why threading configured teams cannot move `BASELINE_HASH`, and a mutation that blurred that boundary would be testing a different claim. Scoped to arena.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

Start accepts a Teams match with everybody on one team. The match then runs to an immediate, unlosable conclusion -- the issue's binding rule is 'Start requires at least two represented teams', and this is the state that rule exists to refuse. It survives every OTHER gate: the slots are assigned, the devices are present, a human is playing, so `versusSetupProblem` returns null and the button enables. The `false &&` form is chosen over deleting the line because it leaves `representedTeams` referenced, so the mutation cannot be mistaken for dead-code removal by a reader of the diff. Killed by the case asserting the refusal in `'teams'` AND its own control -- the identical slots must still be startable in `'ffa'`, without which the test could pass against a build that simply refused Teams outright. Scoped to versus-setup.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

The host claims a gameplay session whether or not one exists -- so the EMPTY state, which is the entire point of issue #427, becomes unobservable. A shell asking 'should I offer Resume' gets yes on a page that has never started a match, and every criterion of the form 'X still works while the host has no active session' loses its second half: the assertions still run, they just stop distinguishing anything. Chosen over `() => false` deliberately, though both are killed: a stuck-false accessor is caught by the two positive cases and reads as an obvious omission, while stuck-TRUE passes the naive 'it reports a session after start()' check and fails only where the emptiness is the claim -- which is the harder shape to notice in review. Four failures across two files, MEASURED: the empty-host cases in session-host.test.ts and the combined route case in route-ui.test.ts, which asserts that driving every application route leaves the host empty. Scoped to those two files; expectFailures counts that scoped run only. COUNT RE-MEASURED for issue #428: 4 -> 7, because the empty host is the page's NORMAL state since #428 rather than a window between sessions, so three more cases assert `hasSession()` is false. The failing SET was compared, not the number renumbered.

Teams becomes selectable at two players, which issue #281's first binding rule forbids by name: 'Teams mode is not a distinct option for two players because it is equivalent to FFA.' Two players on two teams IS free-for-all, and two on one team is a match nobody can win -- which the one-team Start gate then refuses, so the offer becomes a trap rather than a choice. It is a SILENT defect on the shipped pane: the button simply enables, every downstream mode-dependent row renders correctly, and the match starts and plays; what it costs is a mode that means nothing and a refusal the player cannot see the cause of. Killed by the three cases that drive the pane with a real `.click()` -- chosen over `dispatchEvent` deliberately, because a disabled button IGNORES a real click and HONOURS a dispatched one, so only the former measures what a player can actually do. Scoped to hud.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

Dropping from three players to two while Teams is selected LEAVES the pane in Teams -- a mode it no longer offers. The disabled button cannot prevent this state, because the player never touches the mode row to reach it; they touch the player count. The result is a pane whose mode control shows a refused option as chosen, whose Teams-only friendly-fire row is still on screen, and whose Start may be refused by the one-team gate with no visible way to fix it, since the team controls are the thing that would let a player split the sides. Exactly ONE test fails, which is the point of the entry: the offer rule and this consistency rule are separate claims, and a build could satisfy the first while breaking the second -- the disabled button and the forced fallback are not the same guarantee. Scoped to hud.test.ts; expectFailures counts that scoped run only.

find: export const TEAM_COLORS: readonly [number, number, number] = [0xff3b3b, 0x3b82ff, 0x4eff3b];
replace: export const TEAM_COLORS: readonly [number, number, number] = [0xff3b3b, 0x3b82ff, 0xffffff];
why: Team C loses its own hue and renders as the white fallback -- the state that shipped between issue #281's descriptor landing and TEAM_COLORS gaining a third entry.
